title: Trump Cuts US-South Korea Drills After Seoul Declines Iran Role, Kushner Meets Hamas on Gaza Road Map
subhead: Washington signals it will 'substantially reduce' joint exercises on the peninsula days before Ulchi Freedom Shield, linking the move to Seoul's refusal to join US operations against Iran. Separately, Jared Kushner held a rare meeting with Hamas leadership in Egypt to salvage the stalled Gaza disarmament plan.

sections.heading: Washington Downgrades the Korea Alliance
sections.body:
President Donald Trump said the United States will 'substantially reduce' joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his 'very good relationship' with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Seoul's refusal to take part in what he called the 'denuclearisation' of Iran. 'These exercises are not only costly... but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile,' Trump posted on Truth Social, adding it was 'too late to cancel' the annual drills that were due to begin Monday. Seoul responded that the exercises, known as Ulchi Freedom Shield, would proceed 'as scheduled,' while Pyongyang had not commented as of writing, according to the BBC.

The move echoes Trump's 2018 decision to suspend the drills outright during his first-term diplomacy with Kim, and comes days after US, South Korean and Japanese forces detected a second North Korean missile test in as many days. Trump also posted an old photograph of himself with Kim within the last 24 hours. Roughly 28,500 American troops are stationed in South Korea, and military leaders had said about 18,000 South Korean soldiers would take part in the 11-day exercise.
sections.whyItMatters: This ties the future of the US-South Korea alliance directly to Seoul's willingness to back Washington's Iran war, and hands North Korea a diplomatic opening — potentially reviving Trump-Kim talks while loosening the military pressure that has underpinned the peninsula's deterrence.

sections.heading: Kushner Sits Down With Hamas as Gaza Plan Teeters
sections.body:
US envoy Jared Kushner met Hamas's new political chief, Khalil al-Hayya, in Egypt on Sunday — the first meeting at that level since last year's ceasefire — in a push to salvage the US-backed 15-point Gaza road map, according to the BBC and AP. Kushner, fellow envoy Steve Witkoff, Board of Peace director Nickolay Mladenov and former UK prime minister Tony Blair were part of the talks, with Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators also present. A Hamas official told AP the group is committed and waiting for mediators to open a 14-day negotiation period on implementation.

The meeting comes a week after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly rejected the plan, saying 'the IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.' Eight countries — Egypt, the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Turkey, Pakistan and Indonesia — issued a joint statement condemning Israel's rejection and saying it 'threatened' peace efforts, per AP and the BBC. Kushner, Mladenov and Blair are expected to meet Netanyahu on Monday.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is now negotiating directly with the group Israel refuses to recognize, and eight regional powers are publicly siding against Netanyahu. That isolates Israel ahead of its October 27 election and tests whether Trump can override a key ally on the core issue of Hamas disarmament.

sections.heading: Ukraine Launches Largest Drone Attack of 2026
sections.body:
Russia said at least seven people were killed in what officials called the 'largest-scale' attack Ukraine has launched this year — around 822 drones, with 600 aimed at Moscow, whose regional governor called it 'one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory,' per the BBC. A Wildberries logistics warehouse near Moscow was hit, and Ukraine's defence ministry said seven of the ten largest Wildberries distribution centres had been 'disabled.' Kyiv has repeatedly targeted the firm since July, describing its hubs as channels for military supply.

Russia retaliated across Ukraine, killing at least seven and injuring more than 39, with a book market in Kyiv's Pochayna district damaged and air-raid sirens sounding four times overnight. President Volodymyr Zelensky said 13 regions had come under attack this week, with Russia launching more than 1,550 drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs and 62 missiles. The BBC reported the US is reluctant to send more Patriot interceptors because of its own war with Iran, while former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov told CBS that Ukraine should have domestically made ballistic missiles within three to six months.
sections.whyItMatters: The exchange shows the war has become a long-range attrition contest over logistics and missile stockpiles. Ukraine's reliance on home-built drones is being tested precisely as US Patriot supplies dry up, and both sides are betting on the other exhausting its capacity to strike first.

sections.heading: Iran Standoff Nears a Deadline
sections.body:
Al Jazeera's live coverage flagged that the Tehran-US memorandum of understanding is set to expire on Monday, with the terms of that expiry still unclear. In a separate development, Qatar denied Iranian claims that it is holding three Iranian pilots captured after Qatar downed two fighter jets at the start of the US-Iran war, according to the BBC. The denial underscores how Gulf states nominally outside the conflict remain entangled in its consequences.

The standoff continues to ripple through Washington's alliances: Trump's decision on South Korean drills was explicitly tied to Seoul's refusal to join the 'denuclearisation of the Islamic Republic of Iran,' and the BBC noted he has also voiced displeasure at Japan, France and the UK for their hesitance to contribute.
sections.whyItMatters: The expiring MoU is a concrete near-term trigger for escalation or de-escalation. Combined with Washington's evident frustration over allied contributions, the Iran file is now driving changes in US posture far beyond the Middle East itself.

sections.heading: Ebola in DR Congo Becomes the Country's Deadliest Outbreak
sections.body:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has killed 2,325 people, surpassing the toll of the 2018-2020 outbreak to become the deadliest in the country's history, Al Jazeera reported, citing the DRC's National Public Health Institute. Confirmed infections have risen to 4,945, including 101 new cases in the previous 24 hours. The case fatality ratio has climbed from about 20 percent in early June to 46 percent, meaning nearly one in two confirmed cases is now fatal.

The outbreak, declared on May 15 and caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola — which has no approved vaccines or treatments — is the DRC's 17th. UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher warned it is 'the fastest growing on record,' while the WHO's Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said it is on track to eclipse the 2014-2016 West African crisis that killed more than 11,000. Doctors Without Borders' Thomas Parisch said cases are still being detected very late, often only after death, as weak infrastructure, remoteness and conflict near the borders with South Sudan, Uganda and Rwanda hinder the response.
sections.whyItMatters: A rising death rate — not falling — signals the response is losing ground. With no approved vaccine for this strain and conflict disrupting access, the outbreak threatens to become a regional humanitarian emergency, not just a Congolese one.

sections.heading: Zambia's Incumbent Leads as Opposition Alleges Armed Raid
sections.body:
Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema held nearly 59 percent of the vote with more than half of constituencies counted on Sunday, putting him on course for an outright first-round victory, Al Jazeera reported, citing the electoral commission. His closest challenger, Brian Mundubile of the opposition NRPUP, trailed with about a third. A candidate needs more than 50 percent to avoid a run-off.

The count is overshadowed by opposition allegations that armed personnel believed to be from the Zambian army entered Mundubile's Lusaka home on Friday night, firing live ammunition, wounding a member of parliament and removing several people. Zambian authorities had not responded at the time of writing. The EU observer mission described the campaign as 'skewed towards the incumbent,' citing bias in state media and a blurring of government and campaigning, and said vote tallying was suspended for roughly six hours on Friday after reports of violence and stolen ballots. A 57-year-old polling agent was killed near Lusaka on election day.
sections.whyItMatters: Zambia has transferred power peacefully through elections since 1991, making the armed-raid allegation a significant test of that record. A disputed result would carry weight across a region watching whether African elections can still deliver credible outcomes.

bottomLine: Washington's decision to cut US-South Korea drills — explicitly tied to Seoul declining a role against Iran — is the day's most consequential strategic shift: it couples the future of a core Asian alliance to a Middle East war and hands Kim Jong Un an opening. That sits alongside a US push to salvage the Gaza plan by meeting Hamas directly over Israel's objections, and a record Ukrainian drone assault as US Patriot supplies run thin. An expiring US-Iran memorandum, a fast-worsening Ebola outbreak in DR Congo, and a contested Zambian election round out a day defined less by any single battlefield turning point than by Washington reallocating its commitments.
